questions.prompt: A teacher asks a group of pupils coming back from the school trip: "Did you enjoy ……… on the holidays?" One of them answers: "Yes, we enjoyed ……… very much." Which pair fills the two gaps?
questions.explanation: A reflexive pronoun agrees with the subject of its own sentence, and each sentence here has a different subject. The teacher is speaking to a group, so the question takes the plural yourselves. The answer comes from we, so it takes ourselves. That is why the pair with yourself in the question is wrong twice over: the group is addressed, not one pupil. The word ourself does not exist at all — the first person plural reflexive is always ourselves, with -selves. And themselves would put the enjoyment on other people entirely, while the pupil answering is talking about his own group, the one he belongs to.

questions.prompt: In lesson 18, five pupils of an English school give their opinion on school uniforms. Four of them come down on one side. Which pupil says both that she was proud of her uniform and that there are faults in it?
questions.explanation: Sarah is the only speaker who holds both positions at once: she came from a primary school with no uniform, she was proud of hers when she reached secondary school, and she still says there are faults in it as well as advantages. Katie is the one clear opponent — she says the same uniform suppresses their identities. Rachel is for it because it removes the morning decision and the competition between the girls. And Anita is for it because it distinguishes the school and makes it look like a community. Sarah is the one worth remembering, because admitting the other side's point is what makes the rest of an argument believable.

questions.prompt: A notice in the science lab reads: "You needn't turn off the computer. It is programmed to switch off automatically." What is the notice telling you?

options.text: That turning it off is forbidden.
That you ought to turn it off anyway.
That turning it off is not necessary.
That somebody else will turn it off for you.

questions.explanation: needn't says that an action serves no purpose: the machine handles it by itself, so nobody has to. It does not forbid anything — that would be mustn't, and the two are opposites rather than neighbours, which is exactly the confusion the sentence is built to catch. It is not advice either: advice would be should, ought to or had better, and the second sentence gives a reason why the action is pointless, not a reason why it is wise. And nothing in the notice names another person; what switches the computer off is the program, not a member of staff.

questions.prompt: Anita says the uniform makes the girls look really smart, and that people often tell them how nice they look. What does smart mean here?
questions.explanation: smart in this lesson is about appearance: neat, pressed, clean, well turned out. The context settles it, because the very next thing Anita reports is that people say how nice they look. Clever is the other meaning of smart, and it is the one that trips up most readers — but nobody looks clever in a uniform, and the sentence is plainly about how the girls appear. Expensive and fashionable points the wrong way: a uniform is the opposite of fashion, since it is the same for everyone and chosen by nobody. And strict and formal describes the rule that imposes the uniform, not the look the uniform gives.

questions.prompt: Two pupils write about the same forgotten homework. Amine writes "I should have done it last night." His teacher writes "You shouldn't have left it so late." What separates the two sentences?

options.text: The first regrets his own past, the second reproaches another's.
The first is about the past, the second about what is still to come.
The first gives advice, the second forbids.
The first is certain, the second is only possible.

questions.explanation: Both sentences use have plus a past participle, so both look back at something that can no longer be repaired; what changes is who is being blamed. Amine blames himself, which is regret; the teacher blames Amine, which is reproach. Both being in the past, no reading that puts one of them in the future can work — shouldn't have never announces anything to come. Neither is advice, and that is the point of the form: advice would be should do or had better do, and it is only useful while there is still time. And neither measures certainty, which is the work of must, could and couldn't, not of should.
